name: CJC-1295 with DAC

lead: CJC-1295 with DAC is a long-acting analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). People use it in growth hormone peptide stacks hoping for a leaner, more muscular body, faster recovery and better-looking skin.

It mimics GHRH at the pituitary, and the DAC attachment binds blood proteins so its action lasts longer than the version without DAC. That sustained signal is meant to raise growth hormone output, which drives the body-composition payoff. Forum users debate pairing it with ipamorelin or tesamorelin versus choosing the no-DAC version; no trials have tested it for appearance.

paras: Users typically run it as one part of a growth hormone stack, paired with a growth hormone-releasing peptide such as ipamorelin or with tesamorelin. Forum threads mostly compare the DAC version with the shorter-acting no-DAC version. Posters describe changes in body composition, recovery and skin over weeks to months of use.

It is not an approved medicine, and risks in healthy users have not been defined by the sources available. Forum discussions focus on combinations rather than safety data, and products sold online are unregulated.

angle.text: CJC-1295 with DAC is a long-acting GHRH analogue that users stack with ipamorelin for a leaner, more muscular look, better recovery and skin. Sustained GHRH signalling is meant to raise growth hormone output, which feeds body composition. Its effects on appearance have not been tested in trials.

lead: CJC-1295 with DAC (also called DAC:GRF) is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) developed by ConjuChem Biotechnologies. A drug affinity complex (DAC) added to the peptide binds albumin in the blood, which extends how long it stays active compared with shorter-acting GHRH analogues such as the version without DAC (modified GRF 1-29).[1] It is not an approved medicine.

People in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities discuss it as a way to raise growth hormone (GH) and IGF-1 levels in pursuit of leaner, more muscular physiques, better sleep and recovery, and, among younger users, height and facial bone changes.[2][3] The appearance chain users describe runs from more GH and IGF-1, to leaner body composition and faster recovery, to more productive training and a changed physique. It is usually discussed alongside a ghrelin-receptor peptide such as ipamorelin or GHRP-6, and sometimes tesamorelin.[4][5]

Wikipedia reports that in healthy adults a single injection raised plasma GH two- to ten-fold for six days or longer and IGF-1 for about nine to eleven days, with an estimated half-life of six to eight days.[1] Its development for lipodystrophy and GH deficiency reached phase II trials before being stopped after a participant died; the attending physician attributed the death to likely unrelated coronary disease, but the programme was ended as a precaution.[1] The US FDA lists it among bulk substances nominated for compounding and then withdrawn, and has cited serious adverse events including increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction.[6] It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list as a growth hormone secretagogue.[1]
infobox: CJC-1295 without DAC (modified GRF 1-29), tesamorelin, ipamorelin

paras: CJC-1295 belongs to the class of growth hormone secretagogues, which prompt the body to release its own growth hormone rather than supplying GH directly. The class has two families: GHRH receptor agonists, which include GHRH itself, CJC-1295, sermorelin and tesamorelin, and ghrelin receptor agonists, which include GHRP-2, GHRP-6, ipamorelin and the oral compound MK-677.[7] The clinical use of the class is treating growth hormone deficiency, and many members also raise IGF-1, prolactin and cortisol.[7]

The name CJC-1295 is applied to two different things in forum talk and some papers. With DAC it is the long-acting form this article covers. Without DAC, often called modified GRF (1-29), it is a short-acting analogue. Wikipedia notes the two are sometimes wrongly equated in scientific papers.[1]

CJC-1295 is a modified form of GHRH (1-29), the active fragment also known as sermorelin. Compared with sermorelin it carries amino acid substitutions at several positions (D-Ala2, Gln8, Ala15 and Leu27) and a maleimidopropionyl group attached to lysine 30, which forms the drug affinity complex that binds albumin. Its formula is C165H269N47O46 with a molar mass of about 3647 g/mol.[1]

The peptide acts at the GHRH receptor on the pituitary to stimulate GH release, which in turn raises IGF-1. The DAC extension keeps the peptide in the bloodstream for far longer than unmodified GHRH, so IGF-1 stays elevated for days to weeks.[1]

In the 2006 study by Teichman and colleagues in healthy adults, as summarised by Wikipedia, a single injection raised GH two- to ten-fold for six days or longer and IGF-1 half- to three-fold for nine to eleven days, with multiple doses keeping IGF-1 elevated for up to 28 days.[1] A separate 2006 paper by Ionescu and Frohman reported that pulsatile GH secretion persisted during continuous stimulation by CJC-1295.[1] These studies measured hormone levels; they did not measure muscle, fat or appearance.

ConjuChem Biotechnologies introduced the drug affinity complex approach in the mid-2000s; Wikipedia cites papers from July 2005 (Jette and colleagues), March 2006 (Teichman and colleagues) and December 2006 (Alba and colleagues).[1] The company pursued phase II trials in HIV-associated lipodystrophy and growth hormone deficiency. In August 2006 it publicly reported a patient death in the lipodystrophy study and the trial was discontinued. The attending physician considered asymptomatic coronary artery disease with plaque rupture the most likely cause, unrelated to the drug, but research was terminated as a precaution.[1]

It has never been approved for medical use and Wikipedia classes it among abandoned drugs. A related GHRH analogue, tesamorelin, was approved in 2010 for HIV-associated lipodystrophy under the brand Egrifta, where its main effect is reducing abdominal fat.[8] The FDA lists CJC-1295 in a table of bulk drug substances that were nominated for use in compounding and withdrawn, and says compounded products may carry immunogenicity risk. It states that it has identified serious adverse events associated with CJC-1295, including increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction, and that clinical data are limited.[6] The peptide circulates through the online research-peptide market that forum users describe, which the wiki does not cover for sourcing.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On looksmax.org, CJC-1295 with DAC appears in questions about peptide stacks, such as combining it with ipamorelin or tesamorelin. In one thread a user asked whether adding tesamorelin was dangerous; a reply argued there was no point in stacking several GHRH analogues and GHRPs and favoured the no-DAC version with ipamorelin. The reasoning mirrors the pharmacology: ipamorelin acts on the ghrelin receptor and is described by Wikipedia as a selective GH-releasing pentapeptide, originally developed by Novo Nordisk and later tested by Helsinn in phase II trials for postoperative ileus before development stopped for lack of efficacy; it is commonly sold as a research peptide.[9] The FDA lists ipamorelin acetate in category 2 of its 503B interim compounding policy, added on 29 September 2023.[6]

Teenage users ask about the combination for height, sleep and facial bone growth, and ask whether growth plates would be affected; replies mostly redirect to HGH or dispute the height benefit.[2][3] Another user asked about pairing it with teriparatide.[10] On T Nation, older threads from 2011 to 2021 discuss it with GHRP-6 or modified GRF, and one 67-year-old poster described nightly ipamorelin and CJC-1295 with DAC as raising his IGF-1 from a very low level over three months.[4][5][11][12] These are anecdotes, and the wiki does not give dosing or sourcing instructions.

The FDA has cited increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction among adverse events associated with CJC-1295 and notes that peptide impurities and aggregation can raise immunogenicity concerns for compounded injectables.[6] The only phase II programme ended after a participant's death, which the investigator attributed to coronary disease rather than the drug.[1] For the related analogue tesamorelin, Wikipedia lists injection-site reactions, peripheral edema, joint and limb pain, glucose intolerance and diabetes risk.[8] Risks in healthy users taking it for appearance have not been defined by published trials. Because it is a prohibited substance under WADA rules, it also carries sanctions for tested athletes.[1]

No studies found testing CJC-1295 with DAC for muscle, body composition, height or appearance. Early human pharmacology studies in healthy adults, cited by Wikipedia, measured GH and IGF-1 responses over days to weeks.[1] The phase II trial in lipodystrophy and GH deficiency was ended after one participant's death.[1] For the related GHRH analogue tesamorelin, a randomised placebo-controlled trial in HIV-infected patients with abdominal fat accumulation led to its 2010 approval.[8]

lore.intro: CJC-1295 with DAC is discussed on looksmax.org and T Nation as a GH-boosting peptide, usually in stacks with ipamorelin or GHRPs.[4][11]

claims.claim: Using several GHRH analogues together gives a bigger result.
The no-DAC version with ipamorelin is preferable to the DAC version.
It can add height or facial bone growth in teenagers.
It restores low IGF-1 and improves recovery in older users.
Peptides are a safe, natural way to raise GH because they work through the pituitary.
The long half-life of the DAC form makes it more potent than the no-DAC form.

timeline.event: Jette and colleagues publish the first paper on the DAC strategy for GRF, cited by Wikipedia.[1]
Teichman and colleagues report prolonged GH and IGF-1 elevation after single and multiple injections in healthy adults.[1]
ConjuChem reports a patient death in its phase II lipodystrophy trial in August and the programme is discontinued.[1]
Tesamorelin, a related GHRH analogue, is approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy.[8]
T Nation members discuss combining CJC-1295 forms with GHRP-6.[4]
T Nation threads compare modified GRF without DAC with GHRP-6 pairings.[12]
FDA adds ipamorelin acetate to category 2 under its 503B interim compounding policy on 29 September.[6]
looksmax.org threads ask about stacking it with ipamorelin and tesamorelin.
